title: Britain Won A Battle Using A Dead Man's Pockets

segments.narration: A dead tramp in a borrowed uniform fooled Hitler. Britain called it Operation Mincemeat, and it was exactly that cynical.
The man was Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman, dead of rat poison. No family was waiting on news of him.
They built him a life: Captain William Martin, Royal Marines. A fiancée, a ring receipt, an angry bank letter, theatre stubs.
On the thirtieth of April, 1943, a submarine released him into the sea off Huelva, Spain. His briefcase said the Allies were going for Greece.
Two weeks later, decrypted German traffic repeated the lie back. Panzers rolled toward Salonika. The landings hit Sicily.

verdicts.claim: A corpse planted by British intelligence in 1943 deceived German high command about Allied invasion plans.
verdicts.note: 67% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The body was that of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless man who died after ingesting rat poison.
verdicts.note: 92% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: He was given the identity of Captain William Martin of the Royal Marines, complete with love letters and pocket litter.
verdicts.note: False identity Captain (Acting Major) William Martin, Royal Marines, with letters from fictitious fiancee 'Pam', ring receipt, bank overdraft demand and pocket litter.

verdicts.claim: The body was released off Huelva, Spain, on 30 April 1943 carrying letters pointing to Greece and Sardinia.
verdicts.note: Released 30 April 1943 at 4:15 am off Huelva; documents pointed at the Peloponnese and Greek targets with Sicily as cover.

verdicts.claim: A decrypted German message of 14 May 1943 shows the deception worked, and Hitler moved the 1st Panzer Division to Salonika.
verdicts.note: 14 May 1943 decrypt warned of attacks on Sardinia and the Peloponnese; the 1st Panzer Division was transferred to Salonika.
